title: ISRO's GSLV-F17 Launches EOS-05, India's First Geosynchronous Imaging Satellite
excerpt: The 2,367-kg Earth observation satellite will provide near-real-time imaging of the Indian subcontinent from 36,000 km altitude, supporting disaster monitoring and strategic surveillance.
body:
• ISRO successfully launched GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05 (GISAT-1A) from Sriharikota at 2:55 AM IST on September 4, 2026, placing it into a sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit.
  • EOS-05 is India's first dedicated imaging satellite from geosynchronous orbit, capable of imaging the entire Indian landmass every 30 minutes and selected areas every 5 minutes.
  • The 2,367-kg satellite — the heaviest payload GSLV has placed into a geosynchronous transfer orbit — replaces EOS-03, which was lost in a 2021 GSLV-F10 launch failure.
  • The satellite must still complete orbit-raising maneuvers to reach its operational altitude of approximately 36,000 km before it becomes fully operational.

The Indian Space Research Organisation successfully launched its GSLV-F17 rocket carrying the EOS-05 Earth observation satellite early Friday morning, marking India's return to the launch pad after an eight-month gap and delivering a long-awaited geosynchronous imaging capability.

The 51.7-metre-tall rocket lifted off from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, at 2:55 AM IST, placing the 2,367-kg spacecraft into its intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit with a perigee of 170 km and an apogee of approximately 28,934 km.

A Milestone Five Years in the Making

EOS-05, also known as GISAT-1A, represents India's second attempt at establishing geosynchronous Earth imaging capability. The earlier EOS-03 mission was lost when GSLV-F10 failed in August 2021 due to a cryogenic upper-stage anomaly. This launch carries added significance as the 19th flight of India's GSLV programme and extends the vehicle's streak to five consecutive successful orbital injections since that 2021 failure.

"I am very happy to announce that the GSLV-F17 vehicle has successfully and precisely injected the Advanced Earth Observation Satellite 05, the geo-imaging satellite, in the intended and required orbit."

— Dr. V Narayanan, ISRO Chairman

ISRO Chairman Dr. V Narayanan confirmed the satellite's health was "perfectly alright" after separation. Mission Director Thomas Kurian noted that EOS-05 is the heaviest satellite the GSLV has placed into a geosynchronous transfer orbit or sub-GTO orbit, crediting years of extensive preparation by scientists and engineers.

What EOS-05 Can Do

Unlike India's existing low-Earth-orbit imaging satellites such as Cartosat and RISAT, which provide high-resolution snapshots only during periodic orbital passes, EOS-05 is designed to maintain a continuous watch from the geosynchronous belt at approximately 36,000 km altitude.

According to mission specifications, the satellite can image selected areas approximately every 5 minutes and the entire Indian landmass every 30 minutes at 42-metre spatial resolution. It carries multi-spectral and hyper-spectral imaging instruments operating across visible, infrared, and multiple spectral bands.

These capabilities are designed to support disaster management — including cyclone tracking, flood assessment, forest-fire detection, and cloudburst monitoring — as well as agricultural assessment, water-resource management, and strategic surveillance applications.

Strategic Significance

A Department of Space parliamentary reply described EOS-05 as an Earth-observation mission for a "strategic user," indicating the satellite serves national-security purposes beyond civilian applications. Frequent regional imaging from geosynchronous orbit can enhance India's awareness of developments along its land borders and maritime surroundings.

"EOS-05 is a state-of-the-art Earth Observation satellite and India's first imaging satellite from geosynchronous orbit, enabling advanced imaging across visible, infrared, multispectral and hyperspectral bands."

— Jitendra Singh, Science and Technology Minister

Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailed the launch as "a proud moment for our nation," highlighting the growing partnership between ISRO and Indian industry in expanding the country's space capabilities.

The Road to Full Operations

While the launch phase is complete, EOS-05 has not yet reached its operational orbit. The satellite must use onboard propulsion to raise its apogee from 28,934 km to approximately 35,786 km, circularize its orbit, reduce its 19.28-degree inclination, and position itself at its assigned operational longitude.

This distinction matters. In January 2025, GSLV-F15 successfully placed the NVS-02 navigation satellite into its transfer orbit, but the satellite could not complete orbit raising after oxidizer valves failed to open. ISRO has not yet released detailed updates on EOS-05's post-separation orbit-raising maneuvers.

The GSLV-F17 mission also marks ISRO's first launch since the PSLV-C62/EOS-N1 mission in January 2026, ending a prolonged lull in India's launch calendar. With the Gaganyaan uncrewed mission and NVS-03 navigation satellite also in the pipeline, India's space programme enters a busy period through the remainder of 2026.
image_caption: An ISRO GSLV rocket launch. The GSLV-F17 successfully placed the EOS-05 satellite into geosynchronous orbit.
nri_angle: The launch strengthens India's indigenous space capabilities, extending GSLV's streak to five consecutive successes and advancing the country's self-reliant space programme.
